evidence.quote: This is a psychological autopsy study based on qualitative interviews with 63 informants concerning 23 suicides committed by persons aged over 65 in Norway.

Twenty-nine suicides were reported to the project over a period of approximately eighteen months (2006/2007). In two cases the relatives did not want to take part in the interview, in three cases it was impossible to obtain information about the relatives, and in one case the cause of death was uncertain. The study therefore comprises 23 suicides: four women and 19 men aged between 65 and 90.
A total of 63 interviews were conducted for the 23 suicides with 34 relatives, 17 family doctors and 12 home-based care nurses.

evidence.section_title: Ildri Kjølseth, 1 Øivind Ekeberg2 and Sissel Steihaug3
evidence.quote: Oslo, Norway
This is a psychological autopsy study based on qualitative interviews with 63 informants concerning 23 suicides committed by persons aged over 65 in Norway.
This article describes a partial study in a largescale research project on elderly people in Norway who committed suicide.
A total of 172 municipal medical officers in ten counties in southern Norway were asked to report regularly to the project manager all definite suicides among those aged over 65 in their region.
For a study using qualitative methodology, the material comprises a relatively high number of suicides from a geographically large region in Norway constituting both urban and rural areas.

The objective of this qualitative study is to investigate whether the descriptions of elderly people who committed suicide, given by those who knew them, can provide common features that create recognizable patterns, and if so whether these patterns can help to shed light on the suicidal process.
The study therefore comprises 23 suicides: four women and 19 men aged between 65 and 90.

The aim was to have two or three informants for each suicide: close relatives, their family doctor, and the home-based nurse/home help (if relevant). The prerequisite for participating in the interview was that the informants had had close contact with the elderly person – as relatives or as his/her family doctor for a long period (years) – or had had regular contact during the last year of life as a homebased care nurse or home help.

The objective of the interviewer was "to get to know the elderly person" from the informants' narratives, as far as this was possible. The first question was worded as follows: "Can you tell me how you experienced him/her?" The interviewer structured the conversations to cover the topics of major lifetime events, health, aging, personality traits and the social context, including relationships. The open structure of the interviews also encouraged the informants to take up topics they viewed as important in their account of the deceased. The interviews usually lasted approximately two hours and were tape-recorded in their entirety. They took place two to six months after the suicide, as recommended by Beskow et al. (1990).

The history of each elderly person emerged through the narratives of the informants. Suicide is the conclusion of a process that can be illuminated through their history: history reveals connections that can provide a broader understanding of the suicidal process than that acquired through quantitative methods.
This article describes a partial study in a largescale research project on elderly people in Norway who committed suicide.

More than half had told stories of childhood/adolescence characterized by considerable difficulty: illness, loss of close relatives and poverty. 'They had to manage on their own,' the informants said about several of them. Six of the 23 subjects lost one of their parents at an early age (four as infants), three also lost siblings (one through suicide) in their youth. Several had felt rejected by step-parents, and talked of a lack of care after one of the parents died. Many grew up under poor conditions in large families: 'Those who were going to school had to have the clothes without holes.' Illness marked two of them early in life: one had to spend two years in infancy at a tuberculosis sanatorium far away from home. Many of the elderly had acquired education for themselves despite limited financial resources. Three enlisted for active service at a young age. They experienced, and seemed to cope with, severe loss also later in life. Seven of them had lost their spouse relatively early, and three had experienced losing children, one losing two sons in accidents. One who suffered from a serious chronic illness throughout his life looked after four children, two of whom were handicapped, when he found himself alone with them. In the interviews many of the elderly emerged as 'survivors'. Poverty and emotional deprivation on the part of caregivers in childhood did not prevent them from functioning well as adults. They also coped with stress later in adulthood.

They were action-oriented at transitions in life, whether these involved illness or other loss. A doctor told us about one of the elderly who had had a stroke: "He came to me after the stroke, and he'd cycled two thousand kilometers during the summer. He didn't seem like a patient who had just sat down and given up!"One daughter also described her father's behavior after his wife died: "When she passed on he had to cook, iron, wash clothes – everything. But he didn't just sit down. He got on with it straightaway!"They also confronted age by being active. They worked, and they did not give up even though age gradually made them weaker.

This obstinacy could be problematic when the elderly needed help. They would rather manage by themselves without others becoming involved, and they could make it very clear what type of help they wanted.

[page/5/Text/4] Nonetheless the majority became well-established as adults and emerged as vigorous and "achieving" people – many also in later life. They had been markedly actionoriented, even when loss and crises had occurred earlier in life. They seemed to maintain their pressing need to control into old age, and showed little ability to develop new strategies for adapting. [page/5/Text/8] Work had undoubtedly been important for them as a positive force in their lives. They were not afraid of responsibility, and many of them had shown creativity, competence, and considerable work capacity in their field. For many of them the work arena was also a social setting where they could make their contribution to others. The impression from the descriptions was that for them work was exactly that "pleasurable experience" where they found "fulfillment". They put demands on themselves and were very conscientious, but without this appearing forced. [page/6/Text/3] If we relate our findings to these control concepts, the informants tell us about people who had been capable of exercising strong primary control throughout their lives, and the experience of having control was important for their selfesteem. They also coped with loss earlier in life through primary control strategies. Whether they experienced loss of relationships or health at an early or a late age, work and activity was their remedy. [page/6/Text/7] These theoretical control perspectives can serve to give us an understanding of why elderly people with such "patterns" as those described by the informants will be particularly vulnerable when irreversible loss of functional capacity occurs in old age. Their self-image and self-esteem is associated with and dependent on the experience of control, exercised through strength and action. To be able to accept help they must let this control go, which they cannot do. For the same reason they are also unable to develop secondary control strategies. Closedoff feelings and relationships involving distance contribute to this. The overall result may be great loneliness, which further reinforces the pain of the loss of self-esteem. In his theory of "suicide as escape from self", Baumeister describes how loss of self-esteem can cause reactions that lead to the risk of suicide. He claims the starting-point may be that a person no longer manages to live up to his or her own expectations (Baumeister, 1990).
